screens.title: Advanced AAA with TACACS+ and RADIUS
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll master how AAA — authentication, authorization, and accounting — protects both administrative access to network devices and user access to the network. We'll look at TACACS+, the protocol often used to secure administrator logins and command authorization, and RADIUS, the protocol commonly used for 802.1X network access and dynamic policy delivery. You'll learn not only configuration steps on Cisco IOS XE but how to design method lists, implement local fallbacks to avoid lockouts, and integrate RADIUS with Cisco Identity Services Engine for rich authorization attributes. Practical examples include configuring TACACS+ with a shared secret and method lists on a router, and enabling 802.1X on a switch port so that the RADIUS server can assign VLANs dynamically. We'll also highlight common pitfalls — like shared secret mismatches and missing local fallback — and the security practices that reduce risk, such as redundant servers and auditing logs. By the end you'll know when to use TACACS+ versus RADIUS and how to deploy each safely in production.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Advanced AAA
Advanced AAA with TACACS+ and RADIUS
Secure administrator access and user network access using the right protocol, policy, and fallbacks.
In this lesson

You will configure TACACS+ for device administration, implement 802.1X with RADIUS and Cisco ISE, and learn troubleshooting and hardening practices so you avoid lockouts and misapplied policies.

Why it matters

Without correct AAA configurations, administrators can be locked out and users could receive incorrect network access, exposing the enterprise to risk.

Explore Key Topics
TACACS+
Device admin authZ with full-packet encryption and separate AAA functions.
RADIUS & 802.1X
Network access control with attribute-driven VLAN and policy assignment.
Troubleshooting
Shared secrets, fallbacks, and supplicant certificate issues are common failure points.
Concept map
AAA Framework
TACACS+
Admin auth & command authorization
RADIUS
802.1X and attribute-driven policies
Use TACACS+ to gate who can run privileged commands. Use RADIUS to place users into correct VLANs and apply QoS or ACLs dynamically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens we build four measurable abilities. First, you'll be able to distinguish TACACS+ and RADIUS and choose the correct protocol for administrative access versus network access; this matters because the protocols carry different attributes and encryption behaviors. Second, you'll configure a Cisco IOS XE device to authenticate, authorize, and account administrative access using TACACS+, including method lists and shared secrets; having a local fallback prevents accidental lockout. Third, you'll implement 802.1X port-based authentication using RADIUS with Cisco ISE, map identity sources like Active Directory to network profiles, and troubleshoot common supplicant and certificate issues. Fourth, you'll apply troubleshooting techniques and security best practices — strong unique shared secrets, redundant AAA servers, and regular log audits — to reduce operational risk. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual hint and a verified competency milestone so you can validate the skill in a lab environment.

screens.title: What is AAA and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: AAA stands for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting and forms the foundation for controlling and tracking access to network devices and resources. Authentication answers the question who is trying to connect; authorization decides what that identity is allowed to do; and accounting records actions and events for audit and forensic analysis. In practice this means a device will verify credentials against an AAA server, then ask the server whether the authenticated identity may run an elevated command or be placed into a VLAN, and finally record those events so you can later review them. For example, an administrator logging into a router can be authenticated via TACACS+ while the same protocol provides command authorization so only certain commands are allowed. A common misconception is that AAA is only about login credentials — it's not. Authorization and accounting are equally important for ensuring least privilege and traceable actions. In the enterprise, properly implemented AAA reduces risk from unauthorized configuration changes and allows you to correlate user actions with security events. Try to think of AAA as three linked controls that together enforce who can do what and when it happened.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Core Concept
Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
A concise definition and real-world relevance for network control and audit.
Authentication
Verify identity using credentials or certificates. Example: a TACACS+ server validates an admin's username and password or a RADIUS server validates a user's supplicant credentials for 802.1X.
Authorization
Decide permitted actions and assign network policies like VLANs or command sets. Example: send a vendor-specific attribute for VLAN assignment after RADIUS authentication.
Accounting
Record who did what and when for audits and incident response. Example: TACACS+ logs of command executions tied to a username.
Key Takeaway

Treat AAA as an integrated control plane: authentication is not enough unless accompanied by precise authorization and reliable accounting.

Analogy
Think of AAA like a building: authentication is checking ID at the door, authorization is which rooms you're allowed to enter, and accounting is the security camera logs that record where you went.
Common misconception
Assuming authentication fixes all security problems. Without granular authorization and accounting, you cannot enforce least privilege or conduct audits effectively.

screens.title: TACACS+ vs RADIUS
screens.narratorSegment: TACACS+ and RADIUS are both AAA protocols but they solve different problems and have different trade-offs. TACACS+ is Cisco-proprietary, separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct phases, and encrypts the entire packet — features that make it an excellent choice for device administrative access and fine-grained command authorization. RADIUS is an open standard that commonly combines authentication and authorization in one exchange, encrypts only the password, and is broadly supported across vendors — making it ideal for network access control like 802.1X and for carrying rich attribute-value pairs from the server to the network device. A practical example: you would use TACACS+ to restrict which users can configure routing protocols on routers, while you would use RADIUS so a switch can place a user into the correct VLAN and apply QoS based on RADIUS attributes from Cisco ISE. A common misbelief is that you must pick only one protocol; in enterprise networks you typically deploy both and use each where it fits best. The core decision comes down to administrative granularity and encryption needs versus broad vendor support and attribute-driven network access.

keyIdea.text: Use TACACS+ for admin command control; use RADIUS for 802.1X user access and dynamic attributes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Comparison
TACACS+
Cisco proprietary; full packet encryption; separates AAA functions for fine-grained administrative control.
When to use
Device administrative access and command authorization in multi-admin environments.
Strengths
  • Granular exec and command authorization
  • Entire packet encryption
  • Clear audit trail for admin commands
RADIUS
Open standard; combines authentication and authorization; encrypts only the password field; excels at attribute-driven network policy.
When to use
802.1X port authentication, wireless access, and dynamic VLAN/QoS assignment through attributes.
Strengths
  • Wide vendor support
  • Rich attribute-value pairs for dynamic policy
  • Commonly integrates with ISE and AD
Concrete example
A router uses TACACS+ to verify and authorize an admin's enable-level commands while a switch uses RADIUS to assign a wireless user to VLAN 20 based on a RADIUS attribute returned by ISE.
Common mistake
Assuming one protocol fits all. Deploy each protocol where its strengths align with the requirement: TACACS+ for admin control, RADIUS for network access policies.

screens.title: TACACS+ configuration on Cisco IOS XE
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring TACACS+ on Cisco IOS XE follows a clear sequence: enable the AAA framework, define the TACACS+ server and shared secret, create authentication and authorization method lists, and apply those lists to console and VTY lines. Start with the command to enable AAA, which activates the AAA subsystem on the device. Next, use the tacacs-server host command with the server IP and shared key; the shared secret must match exactly on both ends otherwise authentication requests will fail. Create an authentication list that tries tacacs+ first and falls back to local, protecting you from lockout if the server is unreachable. Then create an authorization list for exec and command authorization so the TACACS+ server can control what the authenticated user may do. Apply these lists to the console and VTY lines. A common practice during deployment is to configure and test on a single access line and confirm local fallback before applying globally. Below is a canonical example you can run in a lab; read and type carefully, then test with a simulated server outage to verify the local fallback works as expected.

keyIdea.title: Sequence matters
keyIdea.text: Enable AAA, configure server and shared secret, define method lists, then apply to lines with local fallback.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › TACACS+ Configuration
Canonical CLI example
Type these commands on a lab router. The shared secret must match the TACACS+ server exactly.
! R1 Configuration
enable
configure terminal

! Step 1: Enable AAA new-model
aaa new-model

! Step 2: Configure TACACS+ server
tacacs-server host 192.168.10.10 key Cisco123

! Step 3: Create authentication method list
aaa authentication login TAC_LOCAL_AUTH group tacacs+ local

! Step 4: Apply to console and VTY lines
line console 0
 login authentication TAC_LOCAL_AUTH
line vty 0 4
 login authentication TAC_LOCAL_AUTH

! Step 5: Create authorization method list
aaa authorization exec TAC_AUTHZ group tacacs+ local
aaa authorization commands 15 TAC_AUTHZ group tacacs+ local

! Apply authorization to VTY lines
line vty 0 4
 authorization exec TAC_AUTHZ
 authorization commands 15 TAC_AUTHZ

! Step 6: Configure local fallback user
username admin_local privilege 15 secret cohortia

end
write memory
After applying, attempt to log in with a TACACS+ user. Then simulate the server being unreachable and confirm the admin_local account still grants access.
Troubleshooting callouts
  • Shared secret mismatch leads to immediate TACACS+ rejection and fallback to local.
  • If you forget aaa new-model, the device will not consult external AAA servers.
  • Always test on a console session before applying to remote VTY lines to avoid being locked out.
Key Takeaway

Method lists and shared secrets are the most common root causes for TACACS+ failures; plan fallbacks and test thoroughly.

screens.title: Designing method lists and local fallback
screens.narratorSegment: Method lists are ordered instructions the device follows when performing authentication, authorization, or accounting. When designing method lists, place your preferred external server first and a reliable fallback second. For administrative login you often use a method like: group tacacs+ local — this tries TACACS+ and then local accounts. The reason for this ordering is operational safety: if the TACACS+ server is unreachable, the device can still accept local username/password combinations for console access. A typical mistake is applying a method list that uses only external servers or applying a default list globally without testing; either can result in a locked device. Another important element is applying authorization method lists for exec and command authorization so that command control is enforced by the AAA server. Test each change from a console and from a VTY session; simulate server failure to confirm local fallback works. Also ensure shared secrets are synchronized and that timing and timeout options are sensible so network latency does not cause premature fallback to local authentication. Designing method lists and local fallback means always include a tested local fallback in authentication method lists and validate command authorization separately.. In practical terms, prevent admin lockout with ordered aaa methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Method Lists
Ordered method lists
A clear example shows ordering and the intended fallback behavior.
aaa authentication login TAC_LOCAL_AUTH group tacacs+ local aaa authorization exec TAC_AUTHZ group tacacs+ local aaa authorization commands 15 TAC_AUTHZ group tacacs+ local
Test process: connect to console and apply method list, then restart or block TACACS+ connectivity and confirm local user can still authenticate. Repeat the test on VTY after console validation.
Checklist
  • Validate aaa new-model is enabled.
  • Synchronize shared secrets exactly.
  • Apply and test on console before remote lines.
  • Simulate server failure to verify fallback.
Common pitfall
Relying on a default or global method list without lab testing can leave you without remote access when servers fail.

screens.title: 802.1X, RADIUS, and Cisco ISE integration
screens.narratorSegment: 802.1X is a port-based access control standard where the switch acts as the authenticator and the client device is the supplicant. The authentication is forwarded to a RADIUS server, commonly Cisco Identity Services Engine, which validates credentials against identity sources like Active Directory and then returns authorization attributes. Those attributes can include VLAN assignment, ACLs, or QoS settings that the switch enforces dynamically. In a typical flow, a laptop running a supplicant sends EAP messages to the switch; the switch forwards these to ISE; ISE checks identity and policy and returns an Access-Accept with attributes or an Access-Reject. Common operational issues include supplicant misconfiguration and certificate trust failures when EAP-TLS or PEAP is used. To debug, verify the supplicant configuration, ensure the switch is configured for authentication port-control auto, and check ISE logs for the specific failure reason. Redundancy at the RADIUS layer and careful certificate management are essential for a reliable 802.1X deployment that scales in production networks. 802.1X, RADIUS, and Cisco ISE integration means supplicant → switch (authenticator) → ise (radius) → access-accept with attributes for dynamic policy.. In practical terms, how switch, supplicant, and ise interact for port-based access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › 802.1X & ISE
Authentication flow
A practical outline of messages and responsibilities in a working 802.1X deployment.
Step 1 — Supplicant
Client sends EAP start, challenging the switch to authenticate the session.
Step 2 — Switch (authenticator)
Switch forwards EAP messages to the RADIUS server and enforces port control based on responses.
Step 3 — ISE (RADIUS)
ISE validates the identity source and returns attributes such as VLAN, ACLs, or a reject.
Configuration hints
  • Switch ports: authentication port-control auto
  • Ensure RADIUS server entries and shared secrets match
  • Validate AD integration and ISE authorization rules
Troubleshoot
If VLAN assignment fails, check that ISE is sending the correct vendor-specific attributes and that the switch accepts them.

screens.title: Common issues with RADIUS and 802.1X
screens.narratorSegment: In 802.1X deployments the most common issues fall into three categories: supplicant configuration, certificate trust, and attribute delivery from the RADIUS server. Supplicant problems include disabled 802.1X on the client, incorrect EAP method selection, or expired credentials. Certificate trust issues occur when the client does not trust the RADIUS server certificate chain, which commonly blocks EAP-TLS or PEAP authentication; ensure the proper CA certificate is installed on clients or use a widely trusted CA. Attribute delivery issues happen when the RADIUS server does not send the expected Vendor-Specific Attributes or the switch is not configured to interpret them; this results in successful authentication but no VLAN or policy assignment. When debugging, start at the supplicant and move outward: check client logs for EAP errors, verify switch RADIUS logs for Access-Accept and attribute content, and inspect ISE logs to confirm policy decisions. A useful test is to create a simple static policy in ISE that returns a known VLAN attribute and verify the switch applies it, helping isolate whether the problem is in policy or in attribute transmission. Common issues with RADIUS and 802.1X means verify supplicant configuration, certificate trust, and radius attributes in order to isolate failures quickly.. In practical terms, troubleshooting supplicants, certificates, and attribute delivery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Troubleshooting
Supplicant checks
  • Is 802.1X enabled on the client?
  • Correct EAP method selected?
  • Client credentials valid and not expired?
Certificate checks
  • Does client trust the RADIUS server CA?
  • Are server certificates valid and not expired?

screens.narratorSegment: AAA servers are high-value targets and single points of failure if not designed correctly. Use unique and strong shared secrets for each client-server pair and rotate them on a schedule to reduce the risk of compromise. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll master how AAA — authentication, authorization, and accounting — protects both administrative access to network devices and user access to the network. We'll look at TACACS+, the protocol often used to secure administrator logins and command authorization, and RADIUS, the protocol commonly used for 802.1X network access and dynamic policy delivery. You'll learn not only configuration steps on Cisco IOS XE but how to design method lists, implement local fallbacks to avoid lockouts, and integrate RADIUS with Cisco Identity Services Engine for rich authorization attributes. Practical examples include configuring TACACS+ with a shared secret and method lists on a router, and enabling 802.1X on a switch port so that the RADIUS server can assign VLANs dynamically. We'll also highlight common pitfalls — like shared secret mismatches and missing local fallback — and the security practices that reduce risk, such as redundant servers and auditing logs. By the end you'll know when to use TACACS+ versus RADIUS and how to deploy each safely in production.

Over the next screens we build four measurable abilities. First, you'll be able to distinguish TACACS+ and RADIUS and choose the correct protocol for administrative access versus network access; this matters because the protocols carry different attributes and encryption behaviors. Second, you'll configure a Cisco IOS XE device to authenticate, authorize, and account administrative access using TACACS+, including method lists and shared secrets; having a local fallback prevents accidental lockout. Third, you'll implement 802.1X port-based authentication using RADIUS with Cisco ISE, map identity sources like Active Directory to network profiles, and troubleshoot common supplicant and certificate issues. Fourth, you'll apply troubleshooting techniques and security best practices — strong unique shared secrets, redundant AAA servers, and regular log audits — to reduce operational risk. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual hint and a verified competency milestone so you can validate the skill in a lab environment.

These expanded objectives focus on operational safety and the more nuanced elements you must master. You'll learn to design method lists that prioritize TACACS+ while providing a secure local fallback, which is essential to avoid administrative lockout if a server fails. You'll also configure RADIUS authorization attributes so Cisco ISE can assign VLANs, QoS, or ACLs automatically, and you'll be able to diagnose why those attributes may not be applied. Another objective is mastering certificate trust and supplicant behavior for EAP methods such as TLS or PEAP; certificate issues are one of the most frequent blockers in 802.1X rollouts. Finally, you'll practice auditing and redundancy: schedule log reviews for suspicious AAA events and deploy redundant AAA servers so authentication remains resilient. Each objective includes a short verification step, such as simulating a TACACS+ outage and verifying local login still works.

AAA stands for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting and forms the foundation for controlling and tracking access to network devices and resources. Authentication answers the question who is trying to connect; authorization decides what that identity is allowed to do; and accounting records actions and events for audit and forensic analysis. In practice this means a device will verify credentials against an AAA server, then ask the server whether the authenticated identity may run an elevated command or be placed into a VLAN, and finally record those events so you can later review them. For example, an administrator logging into a router can be authenticated via TACACS+ while the same protocol provides command authorization so only certain commands are allowed. A common misconception is that AAA is only about login credentials — it's not. Authorization and accounting are equally important for ensuring least privilege and traceable actions. In the enterprise, properly implemented AAA reduces risk from unauthorized configuration changes and allows you to correlate user actions with security events. Try to think of AAA as three linked controls that together enforce who can do what and when it happened.

TACACS+ and RADIUS are both AAA protocols but they solve different problems and have different trade-offs. TACACS+ is Cisco-proprietary, separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct phases, and encrypts the entire packet — features that make it an excellent choice for device administrative access and fine-grained command authorization. RADIUS is an open standard that commonly combines authentication and authorization in one exchange, encrypts only the password, and is broadly supported across vendors — making it ideal for network access control like 802.1X and for carrying rich attribute-value pairs from the server to the network device. A practical example: you would use TACACS+ to restrict which users can configure routing protocols on routers, while you would use RADIUS so a switch can place a user into the correct VLAN and apply QoS based on RADIUS attributes from Cisco ISE. A common misbelief is that you must pick only one protocol; in enterprise networks you typically deploy both and use each where it fits best. The core decision comes down to administrative granularity and encryption needs versus broad vendor support and attribute-driven network access.

Configuring TACACS+ on Cisco IOS XE follows a clear sequence: enable the AAA framework, define the TACACS+ server and shared secret, create authentication and authorization method lists, and apply those lists to console and VTY lines. Start with the command to enable AAA, which activates the AAA subsystem on the device. Next, use the tacacs-server host command with the server IP and shared key; the shared secret must match exactly on both ends otherwise authentication requests will fail. Create an authentication list that tries tacacs+ first and falls back to local, protecting you from lockout if the server is unreachable. Then create an authorization list for exec and command authorization so the TACACS+ server can control what the authenticated user may do. Apply these lists to the console and VTY lines. A common practice during deployment is to configure and test on a single access line and confirm local fallback before applying globally. Below is a canonical example you can run in a lab; read and type carefully, then test with a simulated server outage to verify the local fallback works as expected.

Method lists are ordered instructions the device follows when performing authentication, authorization, or accounting. When designing method lists, place your preferred external server first and a reliable fallback second. For administrative login you often use a method like: group tacacs+ local — this tries TACACS+ and then local accounts. The reason for this ordering is operational safety: if the TACACS+ server is unreachable, the device can still accept local username/password combinations for console access. A typical mistake is applying a method list that uses only external servers or applying a default list globally without testing; either can result in a locked device. Another important element is applying authorization method lists for exec and command authorization so that command control is enforced by the AAA server. Test each change from a console and from a VTY session; simulate server failure to confirm local fallback works. Also ensure shared secrets are synchronized and that timing and timeout options are sensible so network latency does not cause premature fallback to local authentication. Designing method lists and local fallback means always include a tested local fallback in authentication method lists and validate command authorization separately.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

802.1X is a port-based access control standard where the switch acts as the authenticator and the client device is the supplicant. The authentication is forwarded to a RADIUS server, commonly Cisco Identity Services Engine, which validates credentials against identity sources like Active Directory and then returns authorization attributes. Those attributes can include VLAN assignment, ACLs, or QoS settings that the switch enforces dynamically. In a typical flow, a laptop running a supplicant sends EAP messages to the switch; the switch forwards these to ISE; ISE checks identity and policy and returns an Access-Accept with attributes or an Access-Reject. Common operational issues include supplicant misconfiguration and certificate trust failures when EAP-TLS or PEAP is used. To debug, verify the supplicant configuration, ensure the switch is configured for authentication port-control auto, and check ISE logs for the specific failure reason. Redundancy at the RADIUS layer and careful certificate management are essential for a reliable 802.1X deployment that scales in production networks. 802.1X, RADIUS, and Cisco ISE integration means supplicant → switch (authenticator) → ise (radius) → access-accept with attributes for dynamic policy.. In 802.1X deployments the most common issues fall into three categories: supplicant configuration, certificate trust, and attribute delivery from the RADIUS server. Supplicant problems include disabled 802.1X on the client, incorrect EAP method selection, or expired credentials. Certificate trust issues occur when the client does not trust the RADIUS server certificate chain, which commonly blocks EAP-TLS or PEAP authentication; ensure the proper CA certificate is installed on clients or use a widely trusted CA. Attribute delivery issues happen when the RADIUS server does not send the expected Vendor-Specific Attributes or the switch is not configured to interpret them; this results in successful authentication but no VLAN or policy assignment. When debugging, start at the supplicant and move outward: check client logs for EAP errors, verify switch RADIUS logs for Access-Accept and attribute content, and inspect ISE logs to confirm policy decisions. A useful test is to create a simple static policy in ISE that returns a known VLAN attribute and verify the switch applies it, helping isolate whether the problem is in policy or in attribute transmission.
